segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finally, brothers and sisters, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run swiftly and be honored, just as happened among you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and that we may be rescued from perverse and evil people, for not everyone has faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Lord is faithful; he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We have confidence in the Lord about you, that you are doing and will go on doing what we command.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: May the Lord direct your hearts toward the love of God and the endurance of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now we command you, brothers and sisters, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to keep away from every brother or sister who lives irresponsibly and not according to the tradition they received from us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not irresponsible among you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying; rather, in labor and toil we worked night and day so as not to burden any of you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is not that we lack the right, but we wanted to give you ourselves as an example to imitate.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even when we were with you, we used to give you this command: if anyone is unwilling to work, they should not eat either.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we hear that some among you are living irresponsibly, not busy working but busybodies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Such people we command and urge in the Lord Jesus Christ to work quietly and eat their own bread.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as for you, brothers and sisters, do not grow weary of doing what is right.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone does not obey our word in this letter, take note of that person and do not associate with them, so that they may be ashamed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yet do not regard them as an enemy, but warn them as a brother or sister.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times and in every way. The Lord be with you all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s. It is the mark in every letter; this is how I write.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and here the whole congregation is in view. “Brothers” alone would suggest to a modern reader that only men are addressed. The generic singular in verses 6 and 15 is likewise rendered “brother or sister.” Several modern translations do the same.

The verb means to hold in high honor or to praise. Applied to a message, it means that the message is received with the respect it deserves, as it had been in Thessalonica. “Be glorified” is the older rendering; some modern translations also use “honored.”

The Greek form can be masculine (“the evil one,” that is, Satan) or neuter (“evil” in general). Most modern translations choose “the evil one,” partly because of the letter’s interest in Satan’s activity in chapter 2. “From evil,” as in the KJV, remains possible. The same adjective describes the “evil people” of verse 2.

notes.phrase: the love of God and the endurance of Christ
notes.traditional: the love of God and the patient waiting for Christ (KJV)
notes.note: Both phrases are ambiguous in Greek. “The love of God” may be God’s love for them or their love for God. “The endurance of Christ” may be the endurance Christ himself showed, the endurance he gives, or steadfast waiting for him. The rendering leaves this open as the Greek does; most interpreters favor God’s love for believers and Christ’s own endurance as the model.

notes.traditional: disorderly (KJV); in idleness / idle (many modern versions)
notes.note: The word describes failing to keep to an expected order or duty; in documents of the period the related verb is used of people who neglect their obligations, such as apprentices who miss work. “Disorderly” now suggests rowdiness, and “idle” fits the context of verses 10–12 but is narrower than the word itself. The same word family is rendered “irresponsible” in verse 7 and “irresponsibly” in verse 11.

Manuscripts differ between “they received” and “you received,” and a few have “he received.” The Greek text followed here reads “they received,” the plural referring loosely to every such brother or sister. The sense is hardly affected.
This is the entitlement of those who preach the gospel to be supported by their hearers. Paul sets out that right at length in 1 Corinthians 9 and there too explains why he chose not to use it.

The Greek says “is not willing,” so the rule targets refusal to work, not inability to work or to find work. The older rendering “would not work” meant the same but is now easily misread. The origin of the saying is uncertain; it resembles proverbial sayings about work, but no exact earlier parallel has been identified.

notes.traditional: working not at all, but are busybodies
notes.note: The Greek is a play on words: the two participles share the same root, roughly “not working but working around,” that is, meddling in what is not their concern. “Not busy … but busybodies” reproduces the pun, as several English versions do.

notes.traditional: the token / the sign in every epistle
notes.note: Ancient letters were commonly dictated to a secretary, and the sender often added the closing lines in his own handwriting. Paul points to his handwriting as the mark of a genuine letter. This is probably connected with the concern in 2:2 about a letter falsely claiming to come from him.

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters (plural address); brother or sister (generic singular)
candidates.reason: It occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and whether to render it inclusively must be decided once or the English will vary chapter by chapter.
The figurative “walk” for conduct is frequent in Paul and John; translators split between “walk” and “live,” and the choice should be uniform.
It recurs across the letters and Revelation and is variously rendered endurance, perseverance, steadfastness and patience.
It is very frequent, with distinct senses (urge, encourage, comfort, appeal) that need fixed English per sense across books.
The word family (ἄτακτος, ἀτακτέω, ἀτάκτως) spans 1 and 2 Thessalonians, and versions split between “idle” and “disorderly”; the two letters must match.
